stories.Headline: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
stories.Summary:
Ai2 released OlmoEarth v1.3, a satellite embedding model, on October 22, 2026, along with precomputed annual embeddings for the entire planet at 10-meter resolution in 64- and 128-dimension versions. The model turns a year of radar and multispectral satellite time series from Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat into one vector for each 10-meter pixel. Alongside it, the company introduced the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, a browser-based tool that lets people explore maps and find similar places without signing in. Until now, the main way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio, which required GPU access and the ability to store imagery.

The release makes the model usable by a wider audience, since a small classifier trained on the embeddings can produce maps for tasks such as crop classification or change analysis. In evaluations across 27 tests on six continents, the 128-dimensional embeddings scored highest on 20 of them, and the 64-dimensional version led on 18. The company also introduced PLANTEUR, a crop-type benchmark for tropical farming. Training the release was cheaper than earlier versions, using 53% of the computing time of v1.2 and 18% of v1, with roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, pretraining data and code are all open, and the embeddings cover 2025, 2024 and 2023 globally, with 2017 to 2022 covering select countries.

Ai2 is the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, which published the model and its technical report on Hugging Face and shared the embeddings through Source Cooperative. The company presented the release as a way for teams to test ideas in seconds rather than running fine-tuning jobs that take hours. Its illustrative example concerns illegal gold mining around La Pampa in Peru's Madre de Dios region, which peaked in 2017 and 2018 and was curbed by Operation Mercurio in February 2019. According to SiliconANGLE, the embeddings show a drop in significant change in the southern mining belt from 34 square kilometers for 2016 to 2020 to 9 square kilometers for 2020 to 2024. The Hugging Face article adds that mining resumed in pockets and that Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve in August 2026.

Articles.Title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
Ai2 releases OlmoEarth v1.3 state-of-the-art AI-ready satellite embeddings for the whole planet

stories.Headline: Crusoe Partners with Araico on AI Cloud in Paraguay
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, the AI factory company, announced on October 22, 2026 a strategic partnership with Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer Araico to build AI compute infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam. The initiative is Crusoe's first dedicated AI Cloud deployment in Latin America and follows its strategy of placing computing near abundant energy sources. Under the agreement, Crusoe plans an initial deployment online in mid-2027, with a path to 106 MW of IT capacity and long-term options to reach about 280 MW in total. The facility will sit next to the Itaipú substation, drawing on one of the most reliable 100% renewable hydroelectric sources in the world. It will serve U.S. cloud customers and growing demand across Latin America through Crusoe Cloud.

Paraguay's President Santiago Peña said the partnership unlocks new value from the country's natural resources and brings jobs, investment, and technology. He described it as a chance for Paraguay to become a regional leader in AI infrastructure. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, who was leading a U.S. business delegation when the deal was signed, called it historic and said it could become the largest private foreign investment in Paraguayan history. Crusoe co-founder Cully Cavness said the company was built to develop digital infrastructure where power is abundant and environmentally aligned. Araico CEO Alejandro Zuccolillo said the deal would turn Paraguay's energy abundance into industrial growth, local jobs, and digital innovation.

Under the division of work, Araico will lead local development and site infrastructure beside the Itaipú substation. Crusoe will manage, operate, and deliver the physical compute for Crusoe Cloud. Crusoe's statement said the project extends its energy-aligned AI infrastructure across North America, Europe, and now Latin America. The companies described the agreement as a step toward deeper digital infrastructure ties throughout the Western Hemisphere. The articles do not give a project cost or describe any further steps beyond the planned 2027 deployment and the scaling options.

Articles.Title: Crusoe Partners with Araico on AI Cloud in Paraguay
Crusoe Partners with Araico to Deploy AI Cloud Infrastructure in Paraguay

stories.Headline: How retirees can protect their data using a data broker opt-out
stories.Summary:
How retirees can protect their data using a data broker opt-out is the kind of step that many older people never take, even though their home addresses, phone numbers and family names can appear on people-search sites they have never visited. A Fox News piece from October 22, 2026 explains that these listings can give strangers a surprisingly detailed picture of a person's life, and it recommends an opt-out as a way to reduce that exposure. The article ties the advice to a tragic case in Minnesota, where investigators found a handwritten list of 11 people-search websites in a suspect's vehicle. The article is careful to note that the list alone did not show whether those sites supplied the victims' addresses.

The Minnesota case involved the June 2025 murders of state lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and the shootings of State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette. The list named sites including TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified, along with notes about which services were free. Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to federal charges on June 11 and was sentenced on July 23 to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years in federal prison, while separate state charges remain pending. The article presents this as an example of how easily personal details can be found, not as proof that any particular site was the source.

The article explains that data brokers gather information from public records, online activity and commercial databases, then combine it into profiles that can include addresses, phone numbers, relatives, property ownership and employment history. For retirees, the piece lists specific risks: scammers using familiar details to make fake financial or family-emergency calls, people who need to protect where they live, and fraudulent Medicare or insurance pitches that sound credible. It advises readers to search their own names, save the pages showing their information, find each site's "opt out" or "remove my information" link, complete any verification steps and check their email for confirmations. It also warns that removal may not be permanent, since listings can reappear, and that removing a listing will not stop every spam call or phishing email.

Articles.Title: How retirees can protect their data using a data broker opt-out
How to Opt Out of Data Brokers (and Stay Out)

stories.Headline: Harvard College students are using newly expanded access to Anthropic’s Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects, and personal tasks after the Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The FAS fir
stories.Summary:
Harvard College students are now using expanded access to Anthropic's Claude for coursework, extracurricular work, and personal projects, following a change the Faculty of Arts and Sciences made over the summer. The FAS first announced in April that it would add Claude to its suite of AI tools while moving ChatGPT Edu to a request-only basis. The transition of these tools to affiliates took place over the summer, and students report their first semester with the FAS-sponsored access. The Crimson reports that some students have built a range of uses for the Claude credits they now receive.

Several students said their preference for Claude reflects their views of the company that makes it. Sean "Brady" Merrill '30 said he chose Claude because Anthropic's leadership did not sign a deal with the Pentagon, a reference to a dispute earlier this year over AI safety safeguards. Conner M. Lewandowski '30 said he felt more aligned with Anthropic's leadership and values than with those of other AI companies. Within courses, the tool is built into some assignments, such as General Education 1201, "Foundations of NeuroAI," and the first-year seminar "Letting Claude Cook," which is taught by Douglas P. Finkbeiner, the FAS senior adviser on generative AI who previously worked for Anthropic. Leonardo Miranda '30 said that course was his first use of the expanded credits and that there is no limit on how many he can use.

Students have also applied Claude to personal and extracurricular work. Santiago D. Revilla '30 described building a website that pulls his Google Calendar and displays the weather for each day to help him plan outdoor activities. Ankit Biswas '30, a research fellow at the Cambridge Boston Align Initiative, said the tool helps him turn ideas into working implementations more efficiently, and Merrill said he has used it to build models for a racing boat club. Biswas said he expects AI tools to become ubiquitous and that Harvard should prepare students for that future, adding that it is broadly good the university is expanding access. The article does not say whether the FAS plans further changes to its AI offerings beyond the April announcement.

stories.Headline: Canva's first public image generation model cements AI ambitions
stories.Summary:
Canva has released its first public image generation model, called Canva Craft, which was built by its research team. The company says the model is meant to compete with similar offerings from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. Coverage of the launch appeared on TechCrunch on October 22, 2026, and on SmartCompany on October 23, 2026. The model is positioned as a step in Canva's broader push into AI.

Canva Craft works in two stages, according to the company. In the first stage, it interprets a user's prompt and builds a plan covering spatial relationships, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and the information used to generate text. In the second stage, it produces an image of up to 2K resolution in as many as 30 aspect ratios for different platforms. Canva says this approach allows accurate object details and legible text, and lets users make precise edits without changing other parts of an image.

Canva trained the model on designs instead of photographs, using human-designed templates from its library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts. Images created with Craft can be turned into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company's image-to-design transformer. Craft is available to all users through the Dream Lab tab and through the Canva API. Canva also plans to support image generation inside third-party chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini through its MCP.

Canva has used several image models on its platform, and TechCrunch notes that the new model will likely help reduce API costs while giving the company better quality and speed control. The company acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai in 2024, and it says researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new model. Canva is also developing two cheaper versions, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which it says will be released soon. The reports add that Canva was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year but cut its 2026 growth forecast, and that outside analysts say its valuation has reportedly fallen from $42 billion to $35 billion.

Articles.Title: Canva's first public image generation model cements AI ambitions
Canva launches Craft, its first image generation model, trained on human-designed templates, available to all users, with plans to support third-party chatbots (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)

stories.Headline: Hyundai Motor Accelerates Semiconductor Localization
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor has been pushing to reduce its reliance on overseas makers of automotive semiconductors, a move it announced on October 21, 2026. The company's Semiconductor Development Group vice president, Kim Jong-sun, made the strategy public at the second Hyundai Mobis Automotive Semiconductor Forum, Auto Semicon Korea, held at the DoubleTree by Hilton Seoul Pangyo in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province. Kim argued that Chinese automakers have begun building their own autonomous driving chips and installing them directly in vehicles, so Hyundai needs to reassess its development speed and cost competitiveness. He noted that the global market is dominated by a few overseas firms, with the top five companies holding 74 percent of the automotive SoC market and 96 percent of the converter market.

To shift that balance, Hyundai plans to standardize semiconductor specifications so that chips from several suppliers can be used interchangeably, which should lower dependence on any single company and reduce development and parts-management costs. It also intends to share performance requirements and development schedules with domestic chipmakers early in the design of new vehicles and to run joint verification for use in real cars. The company will take part as a demand company in government research and development projects to ease the burden on local firms. Hyundai sees openings for domestic companies in high-performance control chips, power management chips and automotive communication chips, as vehicle electronics move toward a central controller. The articles do not give timelines or spending figures for these plans.

Hyundai's concern extends to power semiconductors, which Joo Jung-hong, vice president of the Electrification Design Center, described as making up about 40 to 60 percent of the power module cost in electric vehicles. He said European firms such as Infineon and ST lead in automotive silicon carbide chips, but that China is rapidly building an integrated ecosystem from SiC wafers to finished modules with government backing. Hyundai's assessment is that European companies lead on quality while Chinese companies lead on price and supply, so domestic firms must match both technology and cost. Hyundai and Kia have been applying silicon carbide chips since the Ioniq 5 and EV6 in 2021, and are extending them from 800-volt systems to 400-volt systems. The companies and officials quoted are describing their own strategy, and the articles do not report any external response or what comes next beyond these plans.

Articles.Title: Hyundai Motor Accelerates Semiconductor Localization - Businesskorea
Hyundai Motor Group Opens In-House AI Tech Conference to Outsiders - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI-Trade Warnings Are Ringing From Australia to Texas. How Midterm Elections Could Add to the Concerns.
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, artificial intelligence tools are increasingly shaping how voters find information, according to political experts and new research. Chatbots, media generation services and automated content moderation systems have been rolled out rapidly across major social media platforms, some of them introduced only months before the vote. Researchers say these tools have contributed to biased and inaccurate information about polls and have amplified foreign influence operations. They also say low-quality "slop" content is now feeding the training data that informs chatbot responses.

Tech companies are addressing these dangers inconsistently, if at all, the reporting indicates. Lawmakers and watchdog groups have pressed the companies for details about their testing, their safeguards and the extent of voter interactions with A.I., but say the companies are not sharing enough information. The article notes that A.I. is now being built into nearly every level of the user experience on these platforms. That is a sharp change from 2024, when platforms mostly offered basic image generation tools.

Deen Freelon, a professor of communication at the University of Pennsylvania who studies digital politics, described the situation as uncharted territory. The reporting does not set out a specific requirement or rule that has been imposed on the companies in response. It also does not say what regulators or lawmakers plan to do if the companies continue withholding information. The article is a preview, and the full text was not available in the material provided, so its complete findings and any further details on enforcement cannot be confirmed here.

Articles.Title: AI-Trade Warnings Are Ringing From Australia to Texas. How Midterm Elections Could Add to the Concerns.

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Opella partner on agentic AI content verification platform
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and consumer healthcare company Opella announced on Tuesday, October 21, 2026, that they are partnering to build an agentic artificial intelligence platform to verify health content at scale. The platform will be called Lumen and will consist of 14 specialized agents that check product claims, medical facts, sources and legal mentions. The agents will also advise where content should be placed according to its type and the varying publication channels. Lumen will flag compliance issues, corrections and points where human input is needed.

Opella Chief Growth Officer Alberto Hernandez said that AI is fundamentally changing the speed and scale at which the company can develop and deliver content, and that content production has been scaled by 30 times. He stressed that in healthcare, speed can never come at the expense of trust. Hernandez said the company is using Lumen to help its experts review content faster and make better-informed decisions while keeping human expertise and approval at the center of the process. The articles state that human experts keep the final decision.

The partnership adds to Microsoft's growing set of healthcare AI initiatives. In June, the company announced a strategic collaboration with Mayo Clinic to develop and deploy a frontier AI model designed for healthcare, intended to synthesize diverse clinical data to support earlier diagnoses, more personalized treatment decisions and better patient outcomes. Mayo Clinic will own that model, and Microsoft plans to make it available through Azure Foundry APIs, with initial deployment inside the health system's clinical environment and continuous testing planned. In March, Microsoft also unveiled Copilot Health for consumers, an AI assistant that can review medical records, help patients prepare for doctor appointments and offer personalized insights based on their health data.

Articles.Title: Microsoft, Opella partner on agentic AI content verification platform
Opella, Microsoft partner on AI platform for health content review

stories.Headline: Allooloo Technologies Corp. Launches AI Agent Products for Financial Services Agents: Know Your Product and News
stories.Summary:
Allooloo Technologies Corp. launched AI agent products for financial services on October 23, 2026, announcing what it calls the zones of record, specialist datasets that agents read before a trade, a recommendation or an approval. The first two zones are now live: Know Your Product, which covers every listed issuer in eleven countries and is updated nightly, and News, which carries every filing and release as it lands. The company describes these as adjunct products meant for the AI agents that banks and dealers are adding to their desks. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Vancouver, British Columbia.

The company says the zones are designed to sit alongside existing terminal seats, market data and feeds, rather than replace or re-license them. The Know Your Product zone holds 28,462 listed companies on eleven exchanges and 2.4 million dated disclosures, with each fact signed and linked to the page it came from. The News zone, called Issuerwire.ai, covers 12,489 issuers in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, with 734,154 filings and releases, each headline traced to its source page. Agents can connect over the Model Context Protocol, with the Know Your Product zone at mcp.getissuer.ai and the News zone at mcp.issuerwire.ai, and the company says no account is needed to start. Usage is paid per question, with settlement handled inside each call.

The release is attributed to Matthew Keddy, chief executive of Allooloo Technologies Corp., who argued that agents carry a duty to show where a fact came from, which a human reader never had to prove. He said the company built the zones so agents can cite defensible facts under rules such as Know Your Product, Regulation Best Interest and product governance requirements. The release also lists groups it expects to be affected, including investment dealers and banks, listed issuers, investor-relations desks and newswires, auditors, and several AI laboratories whose models it says already read the zones. Allooloo describes itself as a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner that holds its data in Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services.

The release places the launch within a wider shift in which banks are reducing staffing while adding AI agents, citing JPMorgan Chase and HSBC as examples, and it cites industry estimates for fintech revenue and agentic finance growth. These figures come from the company's own citation of McKinsey and BCG, and the release does not describe any regulatory action or independent review of the products. The article does not say how many customers have adopted the zones or what pricing applies beyond per-question settlement. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Allooloo Technologies Corp. Launches AI Agent Products for Financial Services Agents: Know Your Product and News
‘Know Your Agent’ will be the new rule of the AI age

stories.Headline: 50 emerging leaders selected to foster dialogue and inclusion in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO's Sciences Sector has selected 50 participants from 38 countries for the second edition of the Youth for Peace: UNESCO Intercultural Leadership Programme, according to an announcement dated 21 October 2026. The programme trains young people to use intercultural dialogue to address shared challenges in their communities. This second round moves the focus from the first edition's theme of social cohesion in a mobile world to human connection and dialogue in the age of artificial intelligence, including the opportunities and risks AI presents. The 50 participants, aged 25 to 45, were chosen from 6,786 applicants by an international jury of 26 members, which included UNESCO staff and outside experts in AI and peacebuilding.

The cohort spans Africa, the Arab States, Asia and the Pacific, Europe and North America, and Latin America and the Caribbean, and 52 percent of participants are women. They work in entrepreneurship, research and academia, policymaking, public administration and civil society, with several specialising in AI governance, responsible AI, digital policy, education and technology for social impact. The second edition officially opens with a high-level event on 26 October, after which participants receive mentoring, specialised training and masterclasses on how technology affects social cohesion, trust and peace. Once a project is approved, each grantee receives $10,000 to carry out an intercultural dialogue project in their community.

The article quotes Denise Pires De Carvalho, UNESCO's Assistant Director-General for Sciences, who said that intercultural leadership is more essential than ever as AI changes how people communicate, and who welcomed the cohort as helping to shape a more inclusive and peaceful future. The programme is supported by the Kingold Group. According to the announcement, the programme will close with a Global Youth Dialogue for Peace, where participants will share their experiences with policymakers to inform policy discussions. Afterwards, participants will join an alumni network to keep in touch, share knowledge and continue their peacebuilding work.

Articles.Title: 50 emerging leaders selected to foster dialogue and inclusion in the Age of AI - UNESCO

stories.Headline: Government of Canada expands support for artificial intelligence adoption and commercialization in the Prairie provinces
stories.Summary:
The federal government of Canada has expanded its Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative to support AI adoption and commercialization in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The announcement was made by the Honourable Eleanor Olszewski, Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience and the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada (PrairiesCan). The expansion is part of AI for All, Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, and the article reports it on October 22, 2026. The government describes the step as the next phase after Alberta helped pioneer modern artificial intelligence in Canada. The goal is to make sure Canadian businesses can use the technology and that Canadian AI companies can build, sell and scale their products.

The expansion adds $500 million over five years, raising total federal funding for the initiative to $700 million. Canada's regional development agencies will deliver the program, helping businesses and organizations adopt AI responsibly to improve productivity, competitiveness and resilience. Adoption support will focus on five priority sectors named in the national strategy: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics. The initiative will also help Canadian AI firms find customers, attract investment and scale their offerings, while backing organizations that give small and medium-sized enterprises specialized help.

In the three provinces, PrairiesCan will also strengthen the local ecosystem by supporting incubators, accelerators and other not-for-profit groups. The article attributes the announcement to Minister Olszewski, who is responsible for PrairiesCan, and quotes no other official. It says the program is intended to help businesses across the Prairies become more productive, competitive and resilient while building on the region's existing strengths. The article does not describe any criticism of the initiative or name other parties responsible for carrying it out beyond the regional development agencies.

It also does not say how the funding will be divided among the three provinces. Applications are open now and will be accepted on a continuous basis until December 31, 2029, or until the funding is fully committed. The article encourages applicants to submit expressions of interest as early as possible. Because the initiative runs until the end of 2029 or until the money is spent, the timing of approvals and the size of individual awards are not yet known from the article.

stories.Headline: Sam George Outlines $270m Ghana AI Investment And Warns Against Foreign Data Risks
stories.Summary:
Communication Minister Samuel Nartey George announced on October 22, 2026, that Ghana plans a $270 million investment in artificial intelligence, speaking at the Joy News Digital Economy Forum. He also warned that feeding government data into foreign AI models carries risks. The forum covered the country's digital transformation, technological development and data security. The minister described the investment as a way to use new technology to improve public services and grow the digital economy. His concerns suggest that any adoption of AI needs safeguards to protect sensitive government information.

Public institutions handle confidential records about citizens, public finances, national security and administration, and the reports say sending that material to external AI platforms without adequate protection could expose it to unauthorised access. Uncertainty about how such data is stored and used adds to the problem. The concerns point to the need for clear policies, including stronger data protection standards, secure digital infrastructure and rules on how external technology providers handle government information. The reports note that the $270 million investment also raises questions about how Ghana will build its own AI capacity while protecting national interests. Developing local expertise, supporting domestic technology developers and strengthening local digital infrastructure could reduce reliance on foreign systems.

A separate report from theindependentghana.com adds detail on the infrastructure side. Sam George, the Ningo-Prampram Member of Parliament, said Ghana's first AI data centre would be established within two years, with Phase I providing computing infrastructure for local researchers, universities and businesses that currently buy capacity abroad. He said the government is working through procurement with the Public Procurement Authority to secure the equipment. He also said the centre is only a first step and would not meet all of Ghana's AI needs within the current administration's term. The report notes that Ghana opened a National Data Centre in Accra in January 2016, run by the National Information Technology Agency, while a specialised facility existed at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission from 2010 for nuclear-test monitoring.

The reports make clear that the new centre would be a specialised AI facility rather than a general government data centre, and they leave open how the $270 million will be divided among projects. They do not say what specific data protection rules the government will adopt. Ghana's challenge, as the reports frame it, is to deliver practical benefits to citizens while protecting government information and strengthening digital independence. Whether the infrastructure and safeguards arrive on the stated timeline remains to be seen as procurement proceeds.

Articles.Title: Sam George Outlines $270m Ghana AI Investment And Warns Against Foreign Data Risks – Ghanamma.com

stories.Headline: Building Expertise in AI - USBE and Information Technology
stories.Summary:
Bryan Liles, a senior principal engineer at Amazon Web Services, gave a keynote at the AI NEXTGEN America Conference on the importance of building things in artificial intelligence. He explained how a neuron works, starting with weighted inputs that are summed with a bias to produce a raw output. The network then passes that result through an activation function, which lets it learn complex patterns rather than only linear ones. A loss function compares the prediction with the target value, and training aims to lower that loss. Liles stressed that AI is not a universal solution and that expertise comes from repeated building, feedback, and refinement.

Separately, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology announced new and expanded MIT for America programs to widen access to science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and AI education from kindergarten through community college. The press release cited a striking gap: only 29 percent of U.S. students in grades 9-12 build circuits and just 6 percent enroll in computer science classes, even though 60 percent of high schools offer such courses. The MIT for America Calculus Project will provide calculus tutoring to students in school districts nationwide. Another initiative, the MIT Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education effort, will help teachers bring AI into classrooms and strengthen AI skills in technical vocational schools and community colleges. On October 1, MIT also launched Pathways for AI Training and Hiring, starting with a partnership with Georgia State University to bring workforce-relevant AI training to two-year and four-year colleges.

Cynthia Breazeal, faculty co-director for MIT for America, pointed to the low participation rates in the press release, while MIT President Sally Kornbluth said she looked forward to the growth and evolution of these programs. Career Communications Group, meanwhile, finalized Teacher AI Training Materials and an AI Early Talent Training Certification earlier this year, both aligned with Maryland State Department of Education guidance on AI for K-12 schools. The state's recently enacted Artificial Intelligence Ready Schools Act directs the Maryland State Department of Education to develop guidance, expand professional development, and promote AI literacy across K-12 education. The company's materials cover AI fundamentals, lesson plans, prompt engineering, ethics, bias, privacy, cybersecurity, and digital citizenship. The Maryland Department of Labor partially funded the project, and Tyrone D. Taborn, Chairman and CEO of Career Communications Group, said teachers need the knowledge and resources to teach AI effectively.

Career Communications Group also launched ASCEND Knowledge on Demand, a learning and skills platform within its STEM City USA metaverse, aimed at professionals, veterans, and people seeking career advancement. The platform connects learners with experts in areas including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, energy, healthcare, advanced manufacturing, and technology. It brings together STEM experts, industry leaders, and educators so their knowledge is available on demand. Taken together, these efforts reflect a push by universities, companies, and state governments to build AI skills across both schools and the workforce.

New Initiative launches to Expand STEM and AI Education - USBE and Information Technology

stories.Headline: How soaring AI bills are vexing Wall Street executives
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg reported on October 22, 2026 that soaring artificial intelligence bills are causing concern among Wall Street and other bank executives. Many chief financial officers gave technology teams broad budgets early in the AI rush, and after several surprise bills, controlling costs has become urgent. The problem is most acute in banks, where technology budgets already face pressure from legacy modernization and cybersecurity needs. Agentic AI, which handles complex tasks on its own, is seen as a major source of productivity gains but is hard to budget because the computing power each task uses can vary widely.

Executives have struggled to tie spending to results. Bhavi Mehta, a partner at Bain & Co., said few people in an organization know what a given task will cost, and he argued that cost must be weighed against business value as banks scale up. Only 12 of the 50 largest global banks tracked by the benchmarking firm Evident have publicly tied projected or realized returns to AI adoption. Several US banks raised their AI investment on third-quarter earnings calls, but only a few executives gave precise figures for spending or benefits. Bloomberg spoke with more than a dozen engineers, executives and advisers about how banks are managing the shift from experimentation to deployment.

Banks have adopted several cost-control measures. Deutsche Bank redirected employees whose token use was unusually high toward more productive work instead of cutting them off, and it moved one task to a smaller, specially trained model that cut costs several times over. Banco Santander reserves large frontier models for checking quality and moves proven work to cheaper ones, which lowered the cost of a loan approval process from about €5 to €0.03. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce found its most powerful models could cost C$3,000 per employee a month, so it limited access to a few hundred staff and capped a testing workspace at 250 users with monthly spending between C$4 and C$250. Some lenders are also weighing alternative models, including Chinese ones, though security and governance concerns complicate that choice.

Regulators are watching these developments closely. Canada's banking watchdog asked staff to draft minimum standards for how lenders use frontier AI models, and US Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman warned banks to strengthen defenses against AI-driven threats. Risk executives also worry that deployed AI agents may act unpredictably within bank systems. Former industry executives and advisers say the pace of AI cost increases is far faster than past cloud spending, which took years to bring under control, and the article reports that JPMorgan has set monthly spending limits for certain engineers using Anthropic's Claude Code. The bank's CFO said its annual AI expense was about $700 million, though the figure is hard to pin down because the technology is spread across the entire bank.

Articles.Title: How soaring AI bills are vexing Wall Street executives

stories.Headline: Famous Billionaire Calls AI a Bubble — But That Is Not What His Money Says
stories.Summary:
Ken Griffin, founder of the hedge fund Citadel, said on October 20, 2026, at the firm's Future of Global Markets Conference that artificial intelligence is almost certainly in a speculative bubble. He told Bloomberg that economic transformations often bring bubbles with them. His worry centers on the huge sums flowing into AI infrastructure without a clear sense of future demand. Citing UBS, the articles note that hyperscalers are projected to spend $4.1 trillion on AI infrastructure between 2026 and 2028, nearly triple their spending over the previous six years.

Griffin compared the graphics processing units that power AI systems to airline seats, arguing that once capacity exceeds demand, operators may cut prices because serving another customer costs relatively little. He drew a parallel to the fiber-optic boom around 2000, when telecom companies built far more capacity than the market needed and prices collapsed. He also questioned whether businesses were getting enough value from expensive AI models to justify the cost. Even so, he acknowledged that revolutionary technologies often produce lasting winners, and he said he wished he had kept his Amazon stock during the internet era.

The articles point out that Citadel's own holdings suggest it has not walked away from the sector. According to an amended filing for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, which was submitted on September 2, Citadel Advisors held about $8.6 billion across five AI-linked companies: Amazon at $2.59 billion, Nvidia at $2.36 billion, Microsoft at $1.41 billion, Broadcom at $1.1 billion, and Alphabet at $1.1 billion. During that quarter the firm raised its Amazon share count by 34% and its Microsoft share count by 43%, while cutting Nvidia shares by roughly 37%. The filing also disclosed call and put options on companies including Nvidia and Micron Technology, which can serve as hedges, and the articles caution that the figures are only a snapshot from June.

The articles argue that Griffin's views are not necessarily contradictory, since excess investment can destroy shareholder wealth while also building the foundation for major businesses. They note that Amazon survived the dot-com collapse to become a dominant cloud provider, and that Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Oracle together hold $2.3 trillion in cloud backlog. Griffin also said AI agents have cut some sophisticated Citadel research tasks from weeks to hours. The articles conclude that Griffin is not telling investors to abandon AI but to avoid mistaking a remarkable technology for an investment worth any price.

Articles.Title: Famous Billionaire Calls AI a Bubble — But That Is Not What His Money Says

stories.Headline: Senate Approves Stronger Reporting Requirements for AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material
stories.Summary:
On October 21, 2026, the Pennsylvania Senate voted unanimously to pass House Bill 2474, a measure meant to better protect young people from child sexual abuse material created with artificial intelligence. Senators Tracy Pennycuick, Scott Martin and Lisa Baker sponsored the effort and publicly backed it. The vote came after the bill had been introduced in the House in April 2026. The legislation was sent back to the House to concur on the Senate's amendments.

The bill would require mandated reporters to report every instance of child sexual abuse material they become aware of, including material produced by a minor. Those covered include teachers, childcare workers, healthcare providers and others responsible for caring for children. The language mirrors Senate Bill 1050, which Pennycuick, Martin and Baker introduced in October 2025 and which passed the Senate in November 2025. The bill was also amended to add provisions from Senate Bill 1456, a measure Baker co-authored to make hazing a reportable offense under Pennsylvania's mandatory reporting guidelines. Hazing is not currently treated as child abuse under state law when one child commits it against another.

Pennycuick said children are now being targeted in new ways, and that mandated reporting helps protect them from these acts. Martin said the senators worked with a range of stakeholders, advocates and affected families so that every mandated reporter understands their duties. Baker said clarifying the responsibilities of those who report suspected abuse will help children get the protection and support they need. Baker also said that hazing causes well-documented physical and psychological harm and that adding it as a reportable offense strengthens accountability.

The senators pointed to a sharp rise in AI-generated abuse material being created and shared, including troubling cases in schools. The Senate has previously acted on this problem through Act 125 of 2024 and Act 35 of 2025, which addressed deepfakes and sexual deepfakes. It has also approved Senate Bill 1368, which would ban nudification applications in Pennsylvania, and Senate Bill 1090, which addresses harmful interactions with AI chatbots. With the House still needed to concur on the Senate amendments, the bill's final passage remains pending.

Articles.Title: Senate Approves Stronger Reporting Requirements for AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material - Franklin County Free Press
Senate Approves Stronger Reporting Requirements for AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material - Pennsylvania Senate Republicans

stories.Headline: Idaho Fish and Game website powers down as AI discovers global flaws
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, the Idaho Fish and Game website was replaced with a minimal page that is not working at full capacity. The agency made the switch to a static site to reduce the risk of a security vulnerability. The change came shortly after Scripps News reported that artificial intelligence had found two serious flaws in a programming language used by about 70 percent of the world's websites. In the aftermath of that discovery, many sites around the globe went offline while companies raced to patch the problems.

The agency has not said whether its move was tied to those broader concerns. Officials also said there is no timeline for when the full website will return. Still, the temporary page keeps key information available for hunters and anglers. That includes seasons and rules brochures, public comment opportunities, access to the licensing website, hunter education opportunities, and agency contact information. Anyone who cannot find a specific item on the temporary site is directed to contact a Fish and Game office.

The Idaho Fish and Game agency is responsible for the decision, and its officials announced the change without tying it directly to the global flaws. Scripps News is the outlet that reported the artificial intelligence discovery. The agency's stated reason was the need to minimize potential security vulnerability on its site. Its statement described the move as a precaution. No further explanation of the agency's reasoning appears in the reporting.

The story sits within a wider moment in which the discovery of serious flaws in widely used web software has prompted many organizations to take their sites offline. The articles do not say how long the global patching effort will take or when the Idaho site will be restored. The only concrete next step reported is that the full website remains offline with no set return date. Readers seeking routine information in the meantime can use the temporary page or call a regional office.

Articles.Title: Idaho Fish and Game website powers down as AI discovers global flaws

stories.Headline: Google Is Unlikely to Axe Ex-NPR Host’s AI Voice Use Lawsuit
stories.Summary:
A California state judge has signaled that she will let a lawsuit by former National Public Radio host David Greene against Google LLC move forward. In a tentative ruling, Judge Shella Dean overruled all four of Greene's claims that Google used his voice without permission in an artificial intelligence tool, which had been challenged through Google's demurrer. The judge said she was taking the matter under submission after a contested hearing in Santa Clara County Superior Court on Wednesday. The ruling indicates that the court found each cause of action also stated a claim based on appropriation of Greene's voice and identity.

The articles do not say what the final decision will be, and the full text beyond the tentative ruling is behind a paywall. Greene's complaint centers on the claim that an AI tool used his voice without his consent, which the court's tentative ruling appears to treat as a viable basis for relief. A demurrer is a request to dismiss a lawsuit on the grounds that, even if the facts alleged are true, the claims fail as a matter of law. By rejecting Google's demurrer, the judge would allow the case to proceed to further stages rather than ending it at the pleading stage.

The articles provide limited detail about the specific tool, how the voice was used, or the remedies Greene seeks. Readers are left without the complete reasoning behind the judge's conclusions. Google, as the defendant, filed the demurrer challenging Greene's claims, and the articles present the company's position only through that procedural filing. Judge Dean is the official who issued the tentative ruling and who must decide whether to finalize it.

The articles quote the judge's written language, stating that every cause of action states a claim based on appropriation of Greene's voice and identity and that a demurrer cannot be directed at those claims. Beyond that quoted passage, the articles do not describe further statements from Google or Greene's legal team. The dispute sits within a broader debate over whether voices and likenesses can be used in AI systems without permission, though the articles do not elaborate on that wider context. Whether the judge will issue a final ruling, and when, is not stated.

Articles.Title: Google Is Unlikely to Axe Ex-NPR Host’s AI Voice Use Lawsuit

stories.Headline: The Roles and Missions of Church-Related Institutions in the Era of AI: Humanistic Approaches
stories.Summary:
St. John's University announced a conference titled "The Roles and Missions of Church-Related Institutions in the Era of AI: Humanistic Approaches," to be held on Saturday, October 24, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. in the D'Angelo Center Ballroom on its Queens, New York campus. The event is presented by The Lilly Network of Church-Related Colleges and Universities in partnership with The School of Education. The announcement was posted on the university's website on October 22, 2026.

Attendees were invited to register through an RSVP link on the page. The keynote speakers include Dr. Edmondson, Associate Provost for Continued Learning and founding director of the Learning and Development Initiative at the New Jersey Institute of Technology. His initiative focuses on AI literacy, digital opportunity and workforce capability, and he has delivered more than 100 presentations on artificial intelligence and higher education. He is also the author of ten books, the most recent of which is Remaining Human in the Age of AI, published in 2026.

The second speaker, Dr. Elmoudden, is a professor of communication studies at St. John's whose research examines AI bias, particularly as it relates to culture, minoritized religion and disability. Dr. Elmoudden co-wrote The Future is Now: Empowering Society Through AI Literacy with Jason S. Wrench of SUNY New Paltz. The textbook explains core AI concepts and argues that AI literacy requires ethical awareness and critical thinking alongside technical knowledge. The page presents this material as the basis for the conference's human-centered framing, though it does not describe any formal requirements or policy changes arising from the event.

The speakers' prior appearances in an online video about AI and mental health are also noted on the page. The announcement does not describe any policy change, requirement or new institutional commitment tied to the conference. It frames the event within the broader discussion of how faith-affiliated colleges and universities should respond to artificial intelligence, and it lists the university's other recent education news as context. The page does not say whether additional sessions, publications or follow-up events are planned beyond the October 24 gathering.

Articles.Title: The Roles and Missions of Church-Related Institutions in the Era of AI: Humanistic Approaches

stories.Headline: As AI fears rise, a composer puts it on stage at Symphony Hall
stories.Summary:
Tod Machover, the composer and faculty director of the MIT Media Lab, has written a new classical work called "already and not yet" that premieres Thursday with the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Symphony Hall. During the piece, an AI system listens to the players through microphones and improvises its own music, which is broadcast over a bank of surround-sound speakers. The performance runs through Saturday under the baton of Kent Nagano and is part of the orchestra's week of "Technology and Our Humanity" programming. The article, written by A.Z. Madonna and published October 22, 2026, reports the story as coverage of the premiere. The system was designed by MIT Media Lab PhD researcher Manaswi Mishra, who will control the AI on stage during performances.

Graduate student Ana Schon will mix the sound in the hall. Machover explained that the system can be shaped to stay close to what the musicians play or to make variations and connections between different parts of the sound. Even so, the output is not fully predictable, since Machover knows the general kind of thing it will do but expects it to differ every time. The article notes that Machover, Mishra, and Schon tested the system with BSO musicians at Symphony Hall the week before, and that the players were open and inquisitive.

Machover has said he is not trying to show that human musicians can be replaced by machines. He wants to demonstrate that the technology many people fear can be musical and shaped by and for people. He acknowledged that even saying the word AI to musicians can be frightening, though he described the reaction of the BSO players as encouraging. In his personal life he uses almost no AI tools, does not use chatbots, and manages his own calendar by hand.

He has said that he values attention to detail and dislikes automating most of his work, a view he traces to childhood lessons with his mother, a piano teacher. The article places the premiere within a broader moment of public unease about artificial intelligence, and it presents the work as an effort to model a different relationship between people and the technology. It also points to other recent projects connected to Machover, including a symphony that uses AI and a related reflection on democracy that the BSO is presenting this week. The article does not describe any plans beyond the Thursday-through-Saturday run at Symphony Hall.

Articles.Title: As AI fears rise, a composer puts it on stage at Symphony Hall

stories.Headline: Fresno State faculty integrates AI into curriculum while addressing its limitations
stories.Summary:
Faculty across Fresno State are adding artificial intelligence and machine learning to their courses, the university reported on October 21, 2026. The Department of Computer Science has seven faculty teaching and researching AI, seven AI courses and 14 courses that apply AI tools. It also offers an AI minor and two AI certificates. The Division of Continuing and Global Education offers community members nine professional training courses in AI.

Faculty say students must understand what AI cannot do. Dr. Zareef Mohammed said AI does not think and cannot think, and that it takes existing data and predicts the next plausible word or outcome. Dr. Alex Liu, chair of the Department of Computer Science, said AI is not powerful enough to analyze complex problems and still needs humans for verification and judgment. Dr. David Ruby said fears of runaway AI are overblown, and he puts the risks in the industrial safety category. Liu said he does not worry much about job elimination, because people will work with AI and focus on complex judgment, verification, mentoring and communication.

The immediate challenge is assessing student learning when AI can produce written text. Jason McGensy of the Office of IDEAS said oral exams, blue books and in-class writing are coming back, and more than 300 faculty have taken part in Office of IDEAS AI workshops. Dr. Christian Wandeler recommends integrity by design, setting up assignments so students give personal feedback or draw on their own lived experience. He said teaching students how to use AI matters more than policing it. Dr. Thanos Panagopoulos said motivating students is the most important thing in education.

Liu said the department aims to cover AI literacy and AI tools in general education courses so all majors become AI competent. Ruby said the department is trying to meet demands from industry, academia and students, and that the tools are changing. Panagopoulos is designing a general education course on the social aspects of AI that he hopes to launch in spring 2027. He said students need to understand who controls AI and whose interests it serves.

Articles.Title: Fresno State faculty integrates AI into curriculum while addressing its limitations

stories.Headline: Cybersecurity Month: AI, Deepfakes, and Digital Trust - The University of Maryland, Baltimore
stories.Summary:
The University of Maryland, Baltimore marked Cybersecurity Month with an article published October 21, 2026, by Fred Smith. It says artificial intelligence is quickly changing higher education, health care, research, and the workplace. The same tools that help students and researchers also let cybercriminals create convincing emails, images, voices, and video. One key skill now is checking whether information is real before acting on it.

The article says AI has made phishing emails harder to spot because they can be grammatically correct, well written, personalized, and generated in many languages. It describes deepfakes as images, audio, or video made or altered to look real, and says voice cloning can copy a person from a short sample of their voice. It lists warning signs such as unusual urgency and requests for money, credentials, authentication codes, or gift cards. It advises people to pause, verify through another channel, and confirm unusual requests with a second source.

The article does not name any attacker or victim and reports no specific incident. It says universities are targets because they run on communication, collaboration, and trust, and it describes fake emails from administrators and calls that sound like supervisors. It also says AI helps defenders detect phishing, spot suspicious activity, monitor networks, and improve incident response. The article calls for responsible use of AI and habits such as verifying information before sharing it.

The article presents these steps as preparation for a future in which AI is more deeply integrated into classrooms, research, and administrative work. It says trust can no longer rest only on what people see or hear, and it calls verification the foundation of trust. It gives no dates, figures, or named officials beyond the author and publication date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cybersecurity Month: AI, Deepfakes, and Digital Trust - The University of Maryland, Baltimore

stories.Headline: FSU Law to examine free speech in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
Florida State University College of Law is partnering with the First Amendment Foundation to host a symposium called “Free Speech in the Age of AI” on Thursday, October 22. The event will bring legal scholars, practitioners, and technology experts to Tallahassee for an afternoon of discussion about free speech and government accountability. It is part of FSU Discovery Days, a weeklong celebration of research, creativity, and discovery taking place through October 17 to 24. The symposium will be held in the College of Law’s Main Classroom Building, Room 101.

Registration opens at 1 p.m., and the program begins at 1:30 p.m. In-person attendance is free, with advance registration requested due to limited seating. Online attendance is available for $99 through separate registration. Faculty from FSU and universities across the country will be joined by representatives from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Florida Center for Government Accountability for three panel discussions. Topics will include the use of facial recognition technology to monitor protests and public demonstrations, public access to records related to government AI systems, and legal remedies available when automated decisions infringe on constitutional rights.

Erin O’Hara O’Connor, dean of the FSU College of Law, said people need to understand how the government uses artificial intelligence and what legal protections apply when those uses affect their rights. She said the college is pleased to partner with the First Amendment Foundation to bring scholars and practitioners together to examine these questions and what they mean for the public. Bob Shaw, board chair of the First Amendment Foundation, said the public should be able to understand how government decisions are made, including when artificial intelligence is involved. He said the symposium will examine what access to government records looks like when those records involve AI and how people can seek answers about decisions that affect them.

The event comes as artificial intelligence changes how government agencies conduct surveillance, make decisions, and communicate with the public, and the symposium will examine what those changes mean for the First Amendment and the public’s right to know. The First Amendment Foundation is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for free speech, a free press, and open government in Florida. Through education, training, and advocacy, it helps Floridians understand and exercise their rights to access public records and government meetings. Additional information and registration are available on the event registration page.

stories.Headline: CU Boulder joins Sundance Institute initiative to help filmmakers navigate AI
stories.Summary:
The University of Colorado Boulder has joined the Sundance Institute's AI Literacy Alliance, becoming the latest partner and the only college or university in the group. The alliance supports the AI Literacy Hub, a free online resource that helps independent storytellers understand artificial intelligence and decide whether and how to use it. The announcement was published on October 22, 2026. The hub gathers educational materials so artists can make informed choices while keeping human creativity and artistic expression at the center of their work.

CU Boulder's role builds on its status as the official university partner of the Sundance Film Festival, which will make its Boulder debut in January 2027. The partnership is meant to connect the university's academic expertise and creative community with questions shaping the future of film and storytelling. The resource library covers intellectual property, labor, bias, consent, data collection, fair compensation and environmental impact. It is designed for creators at every experience level, from people seeking an introduction to those already experimenting with new tools. The hub is also meant to grow over time, with planned free live online courses, on-demand learning, events and conversations with artists and experts.

John-Michael Rivera, divisional dean of Arts and Humanities in the College of Arts and Sciences, is among the faculty advising on the initiative. Rivera said AI opens new possibilities for creative expression but that realizing them also requires critical thinking about its risks. He said CU Boulder brings together artists, scholars and scientists who can help filmmakers explore these questions. The university's stated aim is to help them make informed choices that keep human creativity at the center of storytelling.

The AI Literacy Hub is part of a three-year, product-agnostic initiative the Sundance Institute announced in early 2026, with initial support from Google.org. Rather than promote particular tools or a single viewpoint, the initiative aims to give filmmakers the context they need to judge new technologies against their own creative values. The alliance will be part of the 2027 Sundance Film Festival through Sundance Collab's Story Forum, which is scheduled for January 21 to 31, 2027. Other members include the Creators Coalition on AI, Film Independent, The Gotham Film & Media Institute, GFS, the Muslim Public Affairs Council Hollywood Bureau and the National Hispanic Media Coalition. Members will refine and co-develop the resources and give feedback so the hub stays useful as technology and conversations change.

stories.Headline: ISU Lands Grant to build AI-literate Students Through BengalBot Expansion - Idaho State University
stories.Summary:
Idaho State University has received a $300,000, two-year grant through the Accelerate Idaho AI Innovation Awards to expand BengalBot, its locally hosted artificial intelligence system, as announced on October 22, 2026. The project is led by Paul Bodily, an associate professor of computer science, and Jack Bradley, a clinical instructor in industrial cybersecurity engineering technology, who serve as co-principal investigators. Large language models, the technology behind tools like ChatGPT, can struggle with precise math and logic puzzles and may state false information with confidence. Bodily explained that a connector called the Model Context Protocol lets the AI pass those tasks to tools better suited to handle them.

The grant funds three main efforts. First, BengalBot will be built into the Applied AI Certificate and a new bachelor's degree in artificial intelligence sciences, giving 50 to 75 students each year hands-on experience building and auditing AI tools. Second, a writing assistant will be added to Canvas to give feedback on structure and grammar without writing papers for students, with referrals to the ISU Writing Center when needed. Third, a tool called the Stage Hub will be developed with the School of Performing Arts to ease the workload of student stage managers handling rehearsal schedules, costume fittings and cast contacts. Roughly half the funding will go toward a new high-performance server maintained by College of Technology students, with the rest mostly covering student wages.

Bradley, who is interested in the project's control over the tools, said that commercial products such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give the university little say in how they function. The application lists several safeguards, including locally hosted data on ISU-controlled servers overseen by campus IT and network security staff. The writing assistant will undergo an accessibility review and a bias audit before wider use, and English professor Abraham Romney will review a sample of its feedback each semester. Bradley also said the goal is not to automate jobs but to free time for creative work. All source code and curriculum materials will be released publicly under an open license.

Project leaders point to Idaho National Laboratory, which hires more ISU graduates than any other Idaho university, as evidence that skills such as auditing AI outputs match what regional employers need. Bodily expects a theater pilot and limited use in English classes by fall 2027, following a spring semester focused on building and buying hardware. The team also plans to test the writing assistant at another Idaho institution before a broader release. Bradley described the collaboration between STEM and humanities faculty as unusual and said that interdisciplinary mix is what excites him most about the work.

stories.Headline: AI’s role in learning, research, and career exploration—using tools thoughtfully, ethically
stories.Summary:
More than 100 members of the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health community took part in a four-part pilot series on artificial intelligence this fall. The series ran from mid-September to early October 2026 and was covered by Harvard Chan School news on October 21, 2026. Sessions covered generative AI, AI tools for scholarly literature research, large language models for data analysis in public health, and what employers want graduates to know about AI. Jennifer Betancourt, director of educational policy, helped organize the series and said the aim was to build awareness, knowledge and judgment about using these tools thoughtfully and ethically.

The series described generative AI as a machine learning model that can generate content such as text, images or computer code in response to human prompts. It described large language models, including Claude and ChatGPT, as a type of generative AI that generates content based on the probability of what the next word might be. Research and instruction librarian Carrie Wade said these models are good at tasks such as generating emails, creating image captions, summarizing class notes and answering common questions. She warned that they may not always produce true text, that they do not communicate uncertainty, and that they are not designed to say "I don't know."

Wade said AI can provide a good snapshot and some highly relevant information for literature searches but will not be deep or broad, and she noted that the models cannot search research databases because proprietary subscription models limit access. She recommended close attention to any data entered into an AI search, such as unpublished research findings, because all such data becomes part of the model's training. Librarian Alex Cronin showed participants how to use reputable sources such as PubMed alongside AI tools and how to check for hallucinated citations. Lecturer on biostatistics Heather Mattie demonstrated checking AI output in real time and said users should always verify everything.

A final panel of employers, moderated by Sheila Krishnan, director of career and professional development, discussed AI in hiring and the workplace. Sonali Verma of the Clinton Health Access Initiative said people need to be able to stand behind their work and show critical thinking about AI output. Kalé Kponee of the Analysis Group said organizations want to know how AI can be used effectively as a thought partner and critiquing partner, and warned that leaning too heavily on AI outsources learning. The articles do not say what follow-up the school plans after the pilot series.

stories.Headline: Students demonstrate real-world skills through AI solutions
stories.Summary:
Ohio schools are creating real-world learning experiences through artificial intelligence problem-solving. The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce hosted the Ohio AI Impact Student Showcase last week. The event was held in partnership with Intel and the Ohio Educational Service Center Association. It highlighted state efforts to combine emerging technologies with teaching and learning.

Students shared projects with educators, industry leaders and community partners. Their work covered a range of subjects. One project was an app to help students create a career plan. Another was a policy-centered chatbot focused on simplifying information. Students showed how personalized learning can help their peers and the community.

Ohio is the first state in the nation requiring districts and schools to adopt AI policies. These policies address thoughtful instructional use, student and staff responsibility, security and academic integrity. Department Director Stephen Dackin thanked the students for sharing their projects. He also applauded school leaders and educators for their dedication to advancing AI education in Ohio.

The showcase was supported by the Educational Service Center of Central Ohio. It highlighted each school's commitment to excellence in AI education. Eighteen schools and districts were represented at the event, from Buckeye Central Local to Winton Woods City. More to follow.
